name: Olga Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Olga, and thanks for making time. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy furniture and homewares for Nordhaven Home Supply, which sells to about a hundred and fifty independent furniture shops. I source from makers in Poland, Portugal and Vietnam, so I'm on messages all day. I use an AI assistant every morning to translate, compare quotes and draft orders, and then I check everything twice, because a wrong container of chairs costs a fortune. I'm still junior, six years in, since I started after the kids were grown and the firm hired me late.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What happens when the shops pay late?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the sourcing, finding a sofa maker that's good and honest. What wears me out is the tight budget. Mrs Lindqvist (the managing director) squeezes every order, and the shops keep paying us late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say good, because I like predictable. To friends I'd say it's a useful tool and a bubble at the same time. At church I'd say honest work and good habits matter more than any new gadget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm okay with that. The tools I use every day make me quick, and I don't see my job disappearing. What still worries me is the money, because I've got less than a month's wages saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools and I'd get quicker at checking supplier quotes. I'd also open a small online shop selling Portuguese linens and kitchenware at weekends, using my supplier contacts. And I'd put every cent from it into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels pretty comfortable, I'd say. There's a little nervousness about money, but not about the job. I like knowing where I stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you set up the online shop, and how much might it bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peter, my husband, works part-time as a church caretaker and gets a small pension. It helps, but it's not enough on its own. If Nordhaven had a bad year, we'd feel it in a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said if the shops close, your job is at risk. How likely is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The one thing I'd watch in the plateau is the shops. If our customers start closing, because the big online sellers undercut them, my job is at risk no matter what AI does. That's what I worry about at night.

say: I'd say **good**, because I like predictable.
I'd tell friends it's a useful tool and a **bubble** at the same time.
think: I'm okay with it, since the tools I use daily make me **quick**.
The money worries me, with less than **a month's wages** saved.
do: **Keep** using the tools and check supplier quotes faster.
**Open** a small online shop selling Portuguese linens at weekends.
**Put** every cent from the shop into savings.
feel: **Comfortable**, with a little nervousness about money but not the job.
S0.quote: If our customers start closing, because the big online sellers undercut them, my job is at risk no matter what AI does.
fieldNote: She is at ease with AI, so the plateau only worries her through **money** and the shops.
The online shop idea shows entrepreneurial instinct, built on her supplier contacts.
Her husband's small pension helps but doesn't carry the household.

steps.text: Keep using AI to translate and compare supplier quotes
Carry on buying furniture and homewares for the independent shops
Open a weekend online shop selling Portuguese linens and kitchenware
Put every cent from the shop into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's be the first in the trade to use it well. To friends I'd say a person who works and learns will manage, but small firms need fair rules. At church I'd say we should help each other, and that young people need real skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think buying is exactly what shrinks. I use the tools every day, but a better version could do my whole job. I'd be among the last to go, but I'd still be on the list at 58, with low pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd speed up the online shop and use the AI tools to run it, so it earns 400 a month. I'd learn how to set up the ordering automation at Nordhaven myself, so I'm the one who operates it. And I'd start paying 50 a week into a savings account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a fast river. I can swim, but I'd like a bridge to be there. I'm not scared for the work itself, but the ground under my feet isn't firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter Mia and your son Jonas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my daughter Mia, who teaches primary school, that teaching is safer than most. I'd tell my son Jonas to expand his bakery's online orders, because small businesses that use the tools well will do all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be in your written case for Mrs Lindqvist?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Mrs Lindqvist cut the buying team, I'd ask her to let me run the automation. She'd probably say yes if I can show it's saving money. My ask to Mrs Lindqvist is not charity, it's a business case, and I'd put it in writing.

say: I'd say let's be the **first in the trade** to use it well.
I'd tell friends small firms need **fair rules**.
think: Buying is exactly what **shrinks**, and a better version could do my whole job.
I'd be among the last to go, but still on the **list**.
do: **Speed** up the online shop to earn 400 a month.
**Learn** to set up Nordhaven's ordering automation myself.
feel: Like a **fast river**: I can swim, but I'd like a bridge.
S1.quote: My ask to Mrs Lindqvist is not charity, it's a business case, and I'd put it in writing.
fieldNote: She plans to **operate** the automation, which is smart but still depends on her boss's yes.
Anxious since her job could still shrink, though she keeps control through action.
Advice to her children shows faith in small businesses that use the tools well.

steps.text: Learn to set up Nordhaven's ordering automation and offer to run it
Use AI to run the online shop so it earns 400 a month
Pay 50 a week into a savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine to be excited, but nobody can act as if it's all good. At work I'd ask Mrs Lindqvist what the plan is. To friends and at church I'd say we should look after the families who lose out, and not wait for the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be in trouble. If AI can do all thinking work better and cheaper, my job is just a cost to cut. The tools I use every day would be the ones that replace me. There's a kind of irony in that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the online shop hard and hope to reach 800 a month by the end of the second year. I'd cut everything that isn't food, rent and the car, and I'd tell Peter plainly that we're on a tight budget. And I'd ask the church about what help exists for families in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels exciting and awful together. I've always liked new things, so there's a part of me that wants to see what's next. But I'd be scared for my children and for the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your husband Peter that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thing I'd do differently is I'd not wait for anybody. If I'm laid off in 2028, I'd have the shop already running and a little saved. It won't be much, but a head start is better than nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently from your colleagues?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Jonas to put all his energy into his bakery, since food is hands-on and will be safer for the three extra years. And I'd tell Mia to stay in her classroom, because children will always need a person.

say: I'd say it's fine to be **excited**, but nobody can pretend it's all good.
I'd tell friends to look after **families who lose out**.
think: My job is just a **cost to cut**, and the tools I use would replace me.
There's a kind of **irony** in that.
do: **Push** the online shop hard towards 800 a month.
**Cut** everything except food, rent and the car.
**Ask** the church what help exists for families in trouble.
feel: **Exciting and awful** together, scared for my children and the money.
S2.quote: If I'm laid off in 2028, I'd have the shop already running and a little saved.
fieldNote: She expects to lose her job yet **acts** first, the clearest difference from the resistant buyers.
Sees the irony of tools she loves replacing her.
Her advice to Jonas and Mia is shaped by the thinking-first, hands-on-later order.

steps.text: Push the online shop hard towards 800 a month
Cut everything except food, rent and the car
Ask the church what help exists for families in trouble
Tell Jonas to put his energy into the bakery and Mia to stay teaching

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a real chance, if we use it. At work I'd propose a plan for Nordhaven's buying team to share the benefits of the tools. To friends I'd say work hard now, and don't expect anyone to rescue you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd manage. I'd be 63 with a running business on the side, and I'd have used the tools better than most. The money is still the issue, since my savings today are nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year building the online shop into something real, with a proper stock of linens and kitchenware. I'd save 150 a month and I'd learn bookkeeping. And I'd ask Mrs Lindqvist to let me move into supplier relations, which AI would struggle to do for longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like I'm planting a garden I may not harvest. I'd work hard and hope it grows. There's enough time to plant, though, and I'd be glad of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with five years that you couldn't do in two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also invest a little in a printer for labels and a shelf unit for stock. It would be maybe 600, which I'd save for first. I'm not one to borrow when I can wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why save first instead of borrowing for the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robots arriving later wouldn't help me much, because my work is mostly the thinking part. But my stock handling in the shop is hands-on, and I'd keep that part going for the extra years.

say: I'd say five years is a **real chance** if we use it.
I'd tell friends to work hard now and **not wait** for a rescue.
think: I think I'd **manage**, with a business on the side at 63.
The **money** is still the issue, since my savings today are nothing.
do: **Build** the online shop into something real with proper stock.
**Ask** Mrs Lindqvist about moving into supplier relations.
feel: Like **planting a garden** I may not harvest, glad of the time to plant.
S3.quote: I'm not one to borrow when I can wait.
fieldNote: She sees five years as enough to grow her **side business**, but savings remain nothing.
Debt-averse in a traditional way, so she plans to save first.
Chooses supplier relations as the harder-to-automate part of her job.

steps.text: Build the online shop into a real business with proper stock
Save 150 a month for the first year
Learn bookkeeping through an evening course
Buy a label printer and a shelf unit for shop stock

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is generous. At work I'd keep doing a good job and show the young ones how to check the tools. To friends I'd say not to rush, but not to coast either. At church I'd talk about teaching children to be useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be 68, so I'd probably have retired by the time it lands. And I'd have the shop for extra income. I feel better about this one, though I'd still want to put away some real savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work until 65, build the shop slowly and save 100 a month for seven years. I'd teach Jonas how to use the tools for the bakery's orders. And I'd help Mia and her husband save for a house deposit, if I can spare it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels calm. There's enough time to plan, enough to enjoy and enough to put right. I'd say it's the first one where I'd sleep well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for your children in the ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Peter we could finally take that trip to see his cousins in Norway. With ten years, we can do some living as well as saving. It would be a modest trip, but I think we've earned it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you enjoy with Peter that you couldn't in the faster pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, the shop could be a proper retirement income, so I'd leave Nordhaven at 65 with both a pot and a business. That's the dream, and for once it looks possible.

say: I'd say ten years is **generous**, and enough time for the young ones to learn the tools.
I'd tell friends **not to rush**, but not to coast either.
think: I'd be 68 by then, so I'd probably have **retired** by the time it lands.
I'd have the **shop** for extra income.
do: **Work** until 65 and save 100 a month for seven years.
**Teach** Jonas to use the tools for the bakery's orders.
**Help** Mia save for a house deposit if I can.
feel: **Calm**, with time to plan, enjoy and put things right.
S4.quote: With ten years, the shop could be a proper retirement income, so I'd leave Nordhaven at 65 with both a pot and a business.
fieldNote: With a decade, her skills, side shop and retirement timeline line up, so **calm** fits her.
This is the first picture where she imagines enjoying life, not just surviving.
Her plan helps her children as well as herself.

steps.text: Build the online shop slowly into a retirement income
Save 100 a month for seven years
Teach Jonas to use AI tools for his bakery's online orders

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it's too quick for me to turn what I've got into a cushion. My little online shop would have only just started, and my savings are almost nothing. I'd be stuck in the middle.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that the people who work hard and use the tools shouldn't be told they're the problem. A lot of us are doing everything right. We just need time and fair rules for the small guys.

headlineQuote: A lot of us are doing everything right. We just need time and fair rules for the small guys.
portrait: Olga is 58, a junior buyer at **Nordhaven Home Supply**, a furniture wholesaler, with a church-caretaker husband and two grown children.
She is **adaptive**: she uses AI every day and is building a small online shop with her supplier contacts.
She is **traditional**: she values work and savings, dislikes debt and turns to church and family.
Her mood falls to **alarmed** at two years, then eases to anxious, uneasy and calm as time grows.
Her protection is a plan: run the automation at work, build the shop and teach her children.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because her shop would be too new and her savings almost nothing.
whatWouldHelp: **Time** and fair rules for small firms, plus a cushion while her online shop grows.
